## What doing it consciously looks like

Some of it I figured out by thinking. Mostly I learned it by failing at it, and some of it I’m still testing.

Before making love, I want enough honesty to know what we’re walking into. That means talking about jealousy, attraction to other people, what each of us does under stress, old patterns, how recent the healing is, money, and what we want from the other person when things go bad. I’d use situations, not just values: “If X happened, what would you want? What would you probably do?” If all we can give each other is an abstract answer, I assume we probably don’t know yet.

Then stop interviewing each other. Go do ordinary stuff. Ten profound talks in one weekend can feel like depth when really you’ve just talked a lot. Some things I’d rather see than ask about.

After sex, I especially don’t want to let every other decision hitch a ride. Moving in is a separate decision. So is deciding this person should be my life partner. Housing can make separate living hard, but sharing a home creates practical reasons to stay. Put a check-in date somewhere before a crisis chooses the date for you. A wonderful lover can still be a terrible co-parent, community member, or life partner. I also want to catch the moment “I’m taking a chance on her” turns into “she’s the right person” as if those were the same claim. They aren’t.

I want people around us too. Old friends are going to be partial; that’s what friends do. Make some friends who actually know both of you.

And I have to keep doing the things I was doing before she showed up. Being loved isn’t a reason to stop learning to love or regulate myself. If some part of me says, Wait. Something doesn’t fit. I need to ask this, I need to ask it before I talk myself out of it.
